scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document (Carlile 2024, OpenPROMPT study, The Lancet Regional Health - Europe) is a UK cohort study measuring the impact of self-reported Long COVID on health-related quality-of-life using EQ-5D-5L and QALY/QALM methods; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed UK study (OpenPROMPT) that measured how much Long COVID reduces health-related quality of life using patient-reported surveys (EQ-5D-5L) linked to electronic health records. Among 6070 study participants, 24.6% self-reported Long COVID, but only about 6% (described elsewhere in the paper as 'fewer than 10%') had a Long COVID diagnosis recorded in their EHR, showing a large gap between lived experience and formally coded diagnoses. People who self-reported Long COVID had substantially worse quality-of-life scores than those who did not, with losses described in quality-adjusted life-months (QALMs) and compared, in the Discussion, to conditions such as heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease. The study reports no direct medical, non-medical, or monetary cost figures - its burden measures are entirely in quality-of-life (QALY/QALM, EQ-5D utility, odds-ratio) terms, not dollars or pounds.

contextual_issues: Workforce and health-service economic impacts of long COVID are discussed as implications of the HRQoL findings (e.g. 'greater economic costs can be incurred for a substantial part of the UK workforce') but are not quantified in this study itself; the paper cites an external source (Reuschke & Houston 2023) for workforce impact rather than reporting its own cost or productivity-loss estimate.
Caregiver burden/time is not measured or discussed in this document.
Direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), and out-of-pocket patient costs are not reported anywhere in this document.

The low EHR-diagnosis rate relative to self-report is linked by the authors to a possible access barrier ('this has implications if patients are severely impacted by long COVID, but feel unable to fully interact with their primary healthcare'), but this explanation is not independently measured or quantified.
A subset of participants reported HRQoL states 'worse than death' (negative EQ-5D utility), described as representing a minority of the long COVID group but not separately quantified as a percentage.
evidence_gaps: Monetized direct medical cost data (e.g., GP visits, hospital care, medication costs) for long COVID in this cohort or the UK NHS more broadly.
Monetized indirect cost data (lost income, productivity loss in currency terms, caregiving time valued monetarily).
Direct non-medical cost data (travel, paid help).

Longer-term (beyond 3 months) or lifetime HRQoL/QALY trajectories; the 90-day follow-up window cannot be extrapolated into an annual or lifetime QALY-loss figure without an additional assumption this document does not supply.

Disaggregated long-COVID effect estimates separately by sex, ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation/gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status (ethnicity-specific analysis was not possible given the cohort was 95% White).
Clinically validated/confirmed diagnosis of long COVID; status in this study relies entirely on self-report via questionnaire, not independent clinical confirmation.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the three QALM estimation approaches in Table 2 into a single range: complete case analysis (N=510; total QALM 0.81 long COVID vs 0.44 non-long COVID), available case analysis (N=6513; 0.22 vs 0.12), and EHR-diagnosis-defined long COVID (N=6513; 0.22 vs 0.12) differ in population size, case-definition (self-report vs EHR-coded), and missing-data handling, not merely in point-estimate confidence.

Self-reported long COVID prevalence (24.6%, N=1495/6070, survey-based) and EHR/diagnosis-code-recorded long COVID (6%, also described as 'fewer than 10%') are two different case definitions within the same cohort; do not merge or treat them as interchangeable denominators.

OpenPROMPT (UK, self-selected volunteer recruitment via smartphone app/social media/general-practice advertising, general population) EQ-5D scores should not be pooled with the cited comparator studies used for Discussion benchmarking (Walker et al. post-COVID specialist-clinic referrals, Sandmann et al. matched case-control, Sigfrid et al. hospitalised cohort, Moens et al. Belgian online survey, Arab-Zozani et al. Iranian hospitalised cohort) - these differ in population, severity profile, and recruitment route and are presented as qualitative benchmarks, not a pooled estimate.

This document reports no monetary (GBP or USD) cost figures; its HRQoL/QALY-based burden measures (QALM, disutility, EQ-5D utility) must not be combined with or converted into a monetized cost-of-illness figure without a separate, explicitly labeled valuation exercise that this document does not perform.

The headline odds ratio (4.7) and disutility (0.056) are pooled, cohort-wide point estimates, not subgroup-specific effect sizes, even though age, sex, ethnicity and IMD quintile were included as adjustment covariates in the regression models.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Table 1 shows women comprised 70% of self-reported long COVID respondents (1045/1495) versus 61% of the overall cohort (3690/6070), with men comprising 24.9% of the long-COVID group versus 33.8% of the overall cohort. spec.title: Long COVID Quality-of-Life Burden Simulator (OpenPROMPT UK Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulates only the health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) burden measures reported in the OpenPROMPT UK cohort study (Carlile et al. 2024): EQ-5D-5L utility scores, quality-adjusted life-months (QALM) lost (complete-case analysis), odds ratios for reporting HRQoL loss, and the gap between self-reported and EHR-coded Long COVID prevalence in the same cohort. It does not include any monetary cost, workforce-productivity, or caregiving-burden estimate, since the document itself reports none of these in currency terms. A sex/gender skew is noted in documentation (women were 70% of the self-reported Long COVID group vs. 61% of the overall cohort) but is not separately modeled as an input.

takeaway.patient: This UK study found that people who self-reported Long COVID had a noticeably lower health-related quality of life than people without it: an average EQ-5D health-status score (a 0-1 scale where 1 is full health) of about 0.49 versus 0.71, and a larger estimated loss of quality-adjusted life-months (a measure combining how much health status drops and for how long) over the study period. People who self-reported Long COVID also had about 4.7 times the odds of reporting any quality-of-life loss - a significant finding. Fatigue severity was linked to quality-of-life loss, while breathlessness severity was linked to how much loss was reported only among people who already reported some loss, not to whether loss was reported at all. The Discussion compares these quality-of-life losses, in a general way, to conditions like heart failure and multiple sclerosis. Separately, only about 6% of the cohort (described as 'fewer than 10%') had a Long COVID diagnosis formally recorded in their medical chart, versus about 25% who self-reported Long COVID - these measure two different things (how you describe your own symptoms vs. what's coded in your record), and neither is simply the 'more accurate' number; which one matters depends on the question being asked.
takeaway.care: In this cohort, self-reported Long COVID was associated with substantially worse EQ-5D-5L scores and higher odds (OR 4.7, 95% CI 3.72-5.93) of reporting any HRQoL loss than EHR-coded diagnosis rates alone would suggest. Only about 6% of the cohort (the document also says 'fewer than 10%') had a Long COVID diagnosis code in primary-care records, compared with 24.6% self-reporting - a large gap between lived symptom burden and what coded diagnosis captures. Fatigue score (FACIT-F) significantly predicted the odds of reporting HRQoL loss; breathlessness grade (MRC 4-5) significantly predicted the size of the loss among those already reporting loss, but not whether loss was reported at all - these are two distinct, non-interchangeable findings. Once the model adjusted for both breathlessness and fatigue, the odds ratio for Long COVID itself dropped to 1.46 and lost statistical significance (95% CI 0.89-2.38).
takeaway.policy: This OpenPROMPT cohort quantifies Long COVID's burden entirely in HRQoL terms (EQ-5D utility, QALM, odds ratios), not currency: a complete-case QALM-lost gap of about 0.37, an EQ-5D utility gap of about 0.22, and an unadjusted odds ratio of 4.7 (95% CI 3.72-5.93, significant) for reporting HRQoL loss, which weakens to 1.46 (95% CI 0.89-2.38, not significant) once adjusted for breathlessness and fatigue. Separately, EHR-coded diagnosis prevalence (~6%, 'fewer than 10%') was substantially lower than self-reported prevalence (24.6%) in the same cohort, illustrating a measurement gap between formally coded cases and self-reported symptom burden relevant to surveillance interpretation. No monetary cost-of-illness figures are reported in this document; any cost-effectiveness or willingness-to-pay application would require a separate, explicitly labeled valuation exercise this study does not perform.

patient: If this resonates with your own experience, consider asking your clinician how your symptoms (especially fatigue and breathlessness) are being described or documented in your chart, since this study found many people's self-reported symptoms are not reflected in a formal diagnosis note.

If fatigue is a major symptom for you, this study found fatigue severity was linked to quality-of-life loss; if breathlessness is more prominent, it was linked to how severe the loss felt among people already affected, not to whether loss was noticed at all - worth raising both separately with your care team.

You could use the quality-of-life comparisons in this study (to conditions like heart failure or multiple sclerosis) as plain-language context when describing your own impact to family, employers, or benefits processes.
care: This finding - a large gap between self-reported Long COVID (24.6%) and EHR-coded diagnosis (~6%) in the same cohort - may be worth checking against your own practice's coding and referral pathway to see whether symptomatic patients are being formally captured.

Consider whether intake or follow-up for suspected Long COVID routinely includes a fatigue measure (e.g., FACIT-F), since fatigue score significantly predicted the odds of reporting HRQoL loss, distinct from breathlessness grade, which predicted loss severity only among patients already reporting loss.
The authors note EQ-5D-5L may not fully capture fatigue-dominant symptom burden - this could be worth discussing with teams designing symptom-tracking or outcome measures for Long COVID clinics.

Note that the Long COVID-HRQoL association weakened and lost significance once adjusted for breathlessness and fatigue (OR dropped from 4.7 to 1.46); this may be relevant when interpreting multivariable risk models in your own data.
policy: Consider commissioning a separate economic valuation study to monetize this HRQoL/QALM loss into cost-effectiveness terms, since this document provides no monetary cost data of its own.

This cohort's self-report-vs-EHR-coding gap may be worth examining alongside other surveillance data sources to understand how much Long COVID's coded-diagnosis prevalence may undercount self-reported burden in broader populations.

Note that subgroup-specific (sex, age, ethnicity) effect sizes for the Long COVID-HRQoL association are not reported here even though these were adjustment covariates; disaggregated analysis using data sources like MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS could be commissioned to check whether the pooled odds ratio masks subgroup variation.

When citing the 4.7 odds ratio in briefings, also note the adjusted estimate (1.46, not statistically significant) to avoid overstating the independent effect of self-reported Long COVID once breathlessness and fatigue are accounted for.

package.documentation:
This simulator is built from Carlile et al. 2024 (OpenPROMPT study, Lancet Regional Health - Europe), a UK cohort study of self-reported Long COVID and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using EQ-5D-5L surveys linked to electronic health records.

Inputs model the complete-case analysis of quality-adjusted life-months (QALM) lost (Table 2, p.12), mean EQ-5D-5L utility scores (Discussion, p.12), self-reported Long COVID prevalence (Results, p.7; Table 1), EHR-coded diagnosis prevalence (Results, p.7; Discussion, p.13), and unadjusted/adjusted odds ratios for reporting HRQoL loss (Abstract, p.1; Results, p.9), with odds-ratio ranges set to the document's own 95% confidence intervals. All figures describe the OpenPROMPT UK cohort recruited November 2022-July 2023; none are monetary - the document reports no direct medical, non-medical, or income-loss cost figures in currency terms, so none are modeled here.

**Limitations:** The EHR-coded diagnosis prevalence (~6%, described in the document as 'fewer than 10%') is based on primary-care diagnosis/referral codes and likely undercounts the true burden of Long COVID relative to the 24.6% self-reported figure in the same cohort; these measure different things (formally coded diagnosis vs. lived symptom report), not the same quantity measured with different accuracy.

The pooled odds ratio (4.7) and disutility estimate (0.056) are single cohort-wide values; although age, sex, ethnicity, and deprivation quintile were adjustment covariates, the document does not report the Long COVID effect separately by sex, age, or race/ethnicity (the cohort was 95% White). Federal survey data sources such as MEPS, NHIS, and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one. The cohort also showed a sex/gender skew: women comprised 70% of the self-reported Long COVID group versus 61% of the overall cohort (Table 1), and gender was associated with the odds of reporting HRQoL loss in the regression models (Results, p.9), though sex-specific effect sizes for Long COVID itself are not reported separately.

The document also identifies a systemic gap: EQ-5D-5L, a general health-status instrument, may not fully capture fatigue-dominant symptom burden, there is no definitive treatment for Long COVID, and primary-care coding substantially under-captures self-reported cases relative to lived experience - pointing to a mismatch between what the formal care/evidence system records and what patients report experiencing.

Three distinct QALM comparisons exist in the source (complete-case N=510; available-case N=6513; EHR-diagnosis-defined N=6513) with different populations, case-definitions, and missing-data handling; this simulator models only the complete-case version by default and these should not be pooled. The adjusted odds ratio (1.46) did not reach statistical significance (95% CI 0.89-2.38) once breathlessness and fatigue scores were added to the model, unlike the unadjusted odds ratio (4.7, CI 3.72-5.93) - a weakening, not a confirmation of no association. No monetary cost, workforce, or caregiving burden figures are reported in this document and none are modeled here.

spec.title: Long COVID Quality-of-Life Burden Simulator (OpenPROMPT UK Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulates only the health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) burden measures reported in the OpenPROMPT UK cohort study (Carlile et al. 2024): EQ-5D-5L utility scores, quality-adjusted life-months (QALM) lost (complete-case analysis), odds ratios for reporting HRQoL loss, and the gap between self-reported and EHR-coded Long COVID prevalence in the same cohort. It does not include any monetary cost, workforce-productivity, or caregiving-burden estimate, since the document itself reports none of these in currency terms. A sex/gender skew is noted in documentation (women were 70% of the self-reported Long COVID group vs. 61% of the overall cohort) but is not separately modeled as an input.

takeaway.patient: This UK study found that people who self-reported Long COVID had a noticeably lower health-related quality of life than people without it: an average EQ-5D health-status score (a 0-1 scale where 1 is full health) of about 0.49 versus 0.71, and a larger estimated loss of quality-adjusted life-months (a measure combining how much health status drops and for how long) over the study period. People who self-reported Long COVID also had about 4.7 times the odds of reporting any quality-of-life loss - a significant finding. Fatigue severity was linked to quality-of-life loss, while breathlessness severity was linked to how much loss was reported only among people who already reported some loss, not to whether loss was reported at all. The Discussion compares these quality-of-life losses, in a general way, to conditions like heart failure and multiple sclerosis. Separately, only about 6% of the cohort (described as 'fewer than 10%') had a Long COVID diagnosis formally recorded in their medical chart, versus about 25% who self-reported Long COVID - these measure two different things (how you describe your own symptoms vs. what's coded in your record), and neither is simply the 'more accurate' number; which one matters depends on the question being asked.
takeaway.care: In this cohort, self-reported Long COVID was associated with substantially worse EQ-5D-5L scores and higher odds (OR 4.7, 95% CI 3.72-5.93) of reporting any HRQoL loss than EHR-coded diagnosis rates alone would suggest. Only about 6% of the cohort (the document also says 'fewer than 10%') had a Long COVID diagnosis code in primary-care records, compared with 24.6% self-reporting - a large gap between lived symptom burden and what coded diagnosis captures. Fatigue score (FACIT-F) significantly predicted the odds of reporting HRQoL loss; breathlessness grade (MRC 4-5) significantly predicted the size of the loss among those already reporting loss, but not whether loss was reported at all - these are two distinct, non-interchangeable findings. Once the model adjusted for both breathlessness and fatigue, the odds ratio for Long COVID itself dropped to 1.46 and lost statistical significance (95% CI 0.89-2.38).
takeaway.policy: This OpenPROMPT cohort quantifies Long COVID's burden entirely in HRQoL terms (EQ-5D utility, QALM, odds ratios), not currency: a complete-case QALM-lost gap of about 0.37, an EQ-5D utility gap of about 0.22, and an unadjusted odds ratio of 4.7 (95% CI 3.72-5.93, significant) for reporting HRQoL loss, which weakens to 1.46 (95% CI 0.89-2.38, not significant) once adjusted for breathlessness and fatigue. Separately, EHR-coded diagnosis prevalence (~6%, 'fewer than 10%') was substantially lower than self-reported prevalence (24.6%) in the same cohort, illustrating a measurement gap between formally coded cases and self-reported symptom burden relevant to surveillance interpretation. No monetary cost-of-illness figures are reported in this document; any cost-effectiveness or willingness-to-pay application would require a separate, explicitly labeled valuation exercise this study does not perform.

patient: If this resonates with your own experience, consider asking your clinician how your symptoms (especially fatigue and breathlessness) are being described or documented in your chart, since this study found many people's self-reported symptoms are not reflected in a formal diagnosis note.

If fatigue is a major symptom for you, this study found fatigue severity was linked to quality-of-life loss; if breathlessness is more prominent, it was linked to how severe the loss felt among people already affected, not to whether loss was noticed at all - worth raising both separately with your care team.

You could use the quality-of-life comparisons in this study (to conditions like heart failure or multiple sclerosis) as plain-language context when describing your own impact to family, employers, or benefits processes.
care: This finding - a large gap between self-reported Long COVID (24.6%) and EHR-coded diagnosis (~6%) in the same cohort - may be worth checking against your own practice's coding and referral pathway to see whether symptomatic patients are being formally captured.

Consider whether intake or follow-up for suspected Long COVID routinely includes a fatigue measure (e.g., FACIT-F), since fatigue score significantly predicted the odds of reporting HRQoL loss, distinct from breathlessness grade, which predicted loss severity only among patients already reporting loss.
The authors note EQ-5D-5L may not fully capture fatigue-dominant symptom burden - this could be worth discussing with teams designing symptom-tracking or outcome measures for Long COVID clinics.

Note that the Long COVID-HRQoL association weakened and lost significance once adjusted for breathlessness and fatigue (OR dropped from 4.7 to 1.46); this may be relevant when interpreting multivariable risk models in your own data.
policy: Consider commissioning a separate economic valuation study to monetize this HRQoL/QALM loss into cost-effectiveness terms, since this document provides no monetary cost data of its own.

This cohort's self-report-vs-EHR-coding gap may be worth examining alongside other surveillance data sources to understand how much Long COVID's coded-diagnosis prevalence may undercount self-reported burden in broader populations.

Note that subgroup-specific (sex, age, ethnicity) effect sizes for the Long COVID-HRQoL association are not reported here even though these were adjustment covariates; disaggregated analysis using data sources like MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS could be commissioned to check whether the pooled odds ratio masks subgroup variation.

When citing the 4.7 odds ratio in briefings, also note the adjusted estimate (1.46, not statistically significant) to avoid overstating the independent effect of self-reported Long COVID once breathlessness and fatigue are accounted for.

outputs.label: QALM-lost difference: self-reported Long COVID group minus no-Long-COVID group (positive = Long COVID group lost more quality-adjusted life-months; negative would mean the no-Long-COVID group lost more)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's complete-case estimate of how many more quality-adjusted life-months were lost by the self-reported Long COVID group than the no-Long-COVID group; a larger value means a bigger quality-of-life toll in this specific analysis. The document reports two other versions of this comparison (available-case and EHR-diagnosis-defined analyses, both showing a smaller gap of 0.22 vs 0.12 QALM) using different populations and case definitions, which should not be pooled with this complete-case estimate.

outputs.label: EQ-5D-5L utility gap: no-Long-COVID group minus self-reported Long COVID group (positive = Long COVID group has lower health-related quality of life; negative would mean the Long COVID group scored higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between mean EQ-5D-5L utility scores for the two groups in this cohort (about 0.22 points by default); the Discussion compares a gap of this size qualitatively to quality-of-life reductions seen in conditions such as heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease, though those comparator studies used different populations and are not pooled with this cohort's own figures.

outputs.label: Self-reported minus EHR-coded Long COVID prevalence (percentage points; positive = more people self-report Long COVID than have a matching diagnosis code in their health record; negative would mean more people have a diagnosis code than self-report)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap, within the same OpenPROMPT cohort, between two different measurements: how many people say they have Long COVID versus how many have a Long COVID diagnosis code in their primary-care record. It does not mean the self-reported figure is correct and the coded figure is wrong - they measure different things - and the document suggests, without directly measuring, that part of this gap may reflect patients feeling unable to fully engage with primary care.

outputs.label: Odds ratio of reporting any HRQoL loss, self-reported Long COVID vs not (unadjusted model)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's unadjusted odds ratio: people who self-reported Long COVID had about 4.7 times the odds of reporting any loss of health-related quality of life compared with those who did not, a statistically significant result (95% CI 3.72-5.93, not crossing 1).

outputs.label: Odds ratio of reporting any HRQoL loss, self-reported Long COVID vs not (adjusted for breathlessness and fatigue scores)
outputs.interpretation: Once the model additionally adjusted for breathlessness (MRC-Dyspnoea) and fatigue (FACIT-F) scores, this odds ratio dropped to 1.46 with a 95% confidence interval (0.89-2.38) crossing 1, meaning this adjusted association did not reach statistical significance in the document - a weakening of the unadjusted association, not evidence it reverses or disappears.
